notes.title: Choose your gjalfrmarr! - Devlog #23
notes.notes:
Greetings, brave Vikings! 

After the last series of exciting devlogs, in which we presented various aspects of the game's development processes, it's time for more discoveries. Today, we’d like to present you with material that will reveal the secrets of ancient crafts, focusing on shipbuilding and the fascinating types of ships  that the Vikings used. Ready? Therefore, we invite you to read!

[previewyoutube=yDhIooqLjig;full][FILM][/previewyoutube]
The term "gjalfrmarr", derived from Old Norse, means [i]ship[/i] or [i]steed of the see[/i]. Vikings created a variety of ships, broadly divided into two categories: warships and cargo ships. Let's start with the former - the lonships. Despite impressive sizes, reaching about 17.4 meters in length (57 feet) and 2.6 meters in width (8.5 feet), they were still more slender and agile than other Viking ships. Very shallow draught of only 50 centimeters (20 inches), allowed to navigate inland using rivers and dock on most shorelines. That unrestricted mobility often surprised their enemies.

Propulsion consisted of single sail and oarsmen, of which there were usually 16 on board. The length of the oars varied (from 5.3 to 5.85 meters) so that they hit the surface of the water at the same time, accounting for differences in their location relative to the waterline. A characteristic feature of longships was shields attached to the sides, which probably provided protection against wind and waves, although some say that their presence may have been mainly intended to instill fear in enemies when approaching the shores.

In sagas we can find descriptions of gargantuan vessels, such as the Ormurinn langi (Long Serpent), owned by King Óláfr Tryggvason. These giant ships, called drakkars, were much longer and had more oarsmen than typical longships. They served as the flagship units of kings during dynastic wars.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/2674de2470b5b9e89ede1bc88c000cf79f781d03.gif[/img]

As for merchant vessels, let's look at the knarr. They were about 13.8 meters long (45 feet), 3.4 meters wide (11 feet), and had a draught of 84 centimeters (33 inches). Compared to lonships, they required smaller crew and could carry much larger cargo - up to 4.1 tons. Some ocean-going versions, larger and wider, could carry up to 13 tons of goods. These ships had an open construction with partially enclosed decks that contained holes for oars, which were necessary for maneuvering while approaching the shore. However, smaller crew and bigger size translated to being reliant on sail, as the main force of propulsion. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/f26266c72009a4a0377a6163dcb6928c25a05997.gif[/img]

As you can probably guess, ships will be an integral part of our game, and their production will be the responsibility of the Shipwright. Building a ship is both time-consuming and costly. The Shipwright begins by finding an oak tree trunk, which will serve as the keel, the backbone of the ship. Frames, also known as ribs, are then added. The revolutionary clinker planking technique is used, with overlapping planks that are split and fitted together. It's this technique that gave Viking ships such an advantage over other ships. The remaining wooden components include the deck, mast, oars, and rudder. The structure is held together with valuable iron rivets. Lastly, a sail was needed, created on looms (by a Tailor).

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/702eb40d7e71e99a4bef537b7bb11ffb4054340e.gif[/img]

We hope that our devlog has provided you with a lot of valuable information about Viking ships. Let us know how you liked this material, and don't forget to join our community on Discord, where you can stay up to date with the latest news and interact with other Viking enthusiasts!

See you soon! Skål!

notes.title: Nanite technology in Viking City Builder - Devlog #22
notes.notes:
[previewyoutube=mRYKpzptnv0;full][/previewyoutube]
Greetings, Vikings!

We have incredible news to share with you - we're taking our game's graphics to the next level with the introduction of a revolutionary technology developed by Epic Games called [b]Nanite[/b]. In our latest devlog, we'll explore the capabilities of this incredible technology, how it works, and why we're using it in our game, Viking City Builder.

Nanite is an advanced virtualized geometry system that, along with Lumen, powers the heart of Unreal Engine 5. With these cutting-edge solutions, game graphics are evolving beyond our wildest imaginations, ushering in a new era of photorealism and attention to detail. Witness how Nanite, integrated into Viking City Builder, has transformed the humble roof tile of our Longhouse into a breathtakingly realistic work of art.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/9d9df7b18444fc74a122159c99a34ea4ef1af50b.gif[/img]

Thanks to Nanite, Unreal Engine 5 can render billions of polygons in real-time, creating highly-detailed macro and micro-level details that rival those found in blockbuster films. In addition, Nanite uses artificial intelligence (AI) to analyze 3D models in real-time and automatically choose the level of detail (LoD) to be displayed based on the distance of the object from the camera. This means that artists working on 3D models don't need to spend time creating a level of detail (LoD) meshes because Nanite can generate them in just a few seconds. This new technology ensures that performance remains unaffected, allowing gamers to enjoy an incredibly engaging and captivating gaming experience. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/0351905acb2bc79843ab921d74efbd459fcbd84b.gif[/img]

At Viking City Builder, we've always taken pride in our exceptional graphics. With the introduction of Nanite, we're pushing the boundaries even further, setting a new standard for excellence. We're constantly trying to deliver the most immersive and unique experiences for our players, and we believe that Nanite is the perfect tool to bring our vision to life.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/10a99af3f6055b046a2663c6b8d4cee7c3823324.gif[/img]

We hope you've enjoyed learning about Nanite and its incredible capabilities. We'd love to hear your thoughts and feedback, so don't hesitate to leave a comment below. For the latest updates and to connect with other Viking City Builder fans, be sure to join our Discord community.

[url=https://discord.gg/yenDAYP5Ux][img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/2724474b3f8a17c90fc924bcb14e6935f4553e22.gif[/img][/url]

Until next time, skål

notes.title: Seasons - Devlog #21
notes.notes:
[previewyoutube=NMz-whhbAm8;full][/previewyoutube]
Vikings!

Welcome once again to the world of Viking City Builder, where the seasons ebb and flow just like in the real world. As winter gives way to spring, the landscape transforms, offering new opportunities and challenges for your Viking settlement. Read our latest devlog where we’re showing show you the impact of changing seasons on gameplay, as you navigate positive and negative modifications to the game mechanics and visual aspects with each passing season.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/f4b47b787c452425f20373b9e60897586d1aea1b.gif[/img]

Starting from the spring desired by the Vikings, the player will feel stabilized and have the chance to supplement losses after the cruel conditions of winter. Again, there are sources of food that were inaccessible during the winter season, and herbs can now be collected to cure Ill and raise health. Migration can also be expected within this period. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/7f6d4db0708abf32a6e852ef0d92a4fa6457d358.gif[/img]

Summer will be the best time for aggressive expansion both within the village and on the world map since the settlement situation should be already stable as every building will return to normal functioning. This is the period when the player should feel the strongest and most eager to take actions.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/d63fd56776ac8b0557baaa816603c8cf950cb270.gif[/img]

Autumn is a good period to gather resources and harvest food for survival when winter comes. Players can trade their goods for the needed supplies or just to increase the wealth of the settlement. In autumn we will have the materials due to the long availability of all buildings and settlers. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/bc6127a50d02158780560f0f38cba76d49cf7f64.gif[/img]

Winter is the hardest time of the year. Players will be focusing mostly on the survival of their settlement as many of the buildings will not be available, weakening the economy and food production. Providing enough accommodation, heating the houses, having enough food and clothes, and correct management of the settlement, like dynamically assigning professions to the villagers, will be essential to minimize the negative influence of the winter. Unprepared players will be fighting for survival, while those who manage to get ready for this harsh condition will be able to use that time for troop training.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/c42aad4ca7a0a825562119e6bf25ad2db80a2cd4.gif[/img]

We trust that you found our devlog to be informative and that you relished the visuals we've curated for you. Your feedback is highly valued, so please feel free to drop a comment in the section below. 

Additionally, we invite you to join our Discord community, where you can keep abreast of the latest developments and interact with fellow Vikings!

notes.title: Regions system - Devlog #20
notes.notes:
[previewyoutube=uL_VVYZ3CTQ;full][/previewyoutube]

Hello fellow Vikings! 

Welcome to our latest devlog. Today, we'd like to introduce you to one of the exciting mechanical aspects of designing Viking City Builder - the Regions system. In this devlog, you'll learn what this feature is and how it can be used in our game. 

Alright, let's get down to business. This feature allows us to scan objects within the area to check if that part of the map is considered a region, like counting trees to define if there are enough of them to create a “forest” zone. Of course, we can have many regions of the same type, like, forests near the sea, forests up the hill, etc. Those regions of the same type can fuse into a larger one.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/91651a7c15dceb46043572f21b77996e1620c470.gif[/img]

The basic planned regions consist of forests, settlements, and the sea. Each region affects some aspects of the game like currently playing ambient sounds and functionality of some buildings that require a specific region to work.

Let’s look further into the most basic example of the forest region. This region is defined by the number of trees, which can increase and decrease depending on the player's actions. This area provides wood logs for logging huts, animals for a hunting lodge, fruits and tinder for a foragers' shack, and herbs for the herb dryer.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/b54068f2ce10b0472ea349fe38ac4adbdcf010e4.gif[/img]

For the difference, the sea is a region pre-defined by the map geography (distance from the shore) and can't be changed by the player. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/8178d936cf5ff079c54b86bcc0b5e8a44df207f3.gif[/img]

The settlement area range is mostly dependent on the player since its range grows with the number of buildings within the area.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/abe49fbab1a63b1ae2ef65a316d3a10c3af19ba1.gif[/img]

We hope you found this devlog informative and enjoyed the visual materials we've prepared for you. We'd love to hear your thoughts, so don't hesitate to leave a comment below. Also, be sure to join our Discord community to stay up to date on the latest news and connect with other Viking City Builder enthusiasts.

Thanks again for your support, and we'll see you in the next devlog!

notes.title: Mechanics of product selection in industrial buildings - Devlog #19
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/ca1793d63924548f995b17e8dea8e4d139981166.png[/img]

Greetings fellow Vikings!

This time we'll look at the mechanics of product selection in some of the industrial buildings, as one workshop can produce several different goods. Still, only one product can be crafted at a time.

A prudent leader is able to adapt the current production of goods to the ever-changing needs of the village, so the player can change the products being produced at any time during the building's existence. Of course, before the change can take place, the currently ongoing task must first end.

With this arrangement, the village leader will be able to respond relatively quickly to emerging village issues and society needs.

For example, we can look at the products created by a Tailor. Here, the player, depending on the economic situation of the village, can craft clothes that are cheap to produce, or their more desirable and more expensive, exclusive versions. If the player finds that the demand for clothing isn't high, or simply wishes to prepare for ship production, he can choose to produce sails.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/72350185d795425af021410bbfc256016132ab64.gif[/img]

When talking about the possibilities of responding to changing settlement needs, we also can't overlook the function of demolishing buildings.

Once the player determines that an already functioning building is no longer needed, he can start the demolition procedure.

The process will be the reverse of the construction stages, where some of the materials used to create the building will be recovered. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/1c31483f18fce3f20bae8342e7e976cb3d5b6794.gif[/img]

The player can cancel the demolition, but only until the workers have started their work. When this happens, the building will already be demolished in the next few steps.

Any goods held by the building, if they haven't already been used, will be returned. Those that were already in use, such as clothes, will be lost as demolition begins.

If a player wishes to demolish an industrial building, then the process can only begin once the currently ongoing product crafting has been completed.

When a residential building is to be demolished, its inhabitants move to other houses or become homeless.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/38e337ef6fc8d9c2876b32b923bf37d5e1e77c3b.gif[/img]

Thanks for your attention! We hope you also liked this kind of material. Let us know what you think and don't forget to join our Discord!

Hello fellow Vikings!

2023 is looming on the horizon and it's an excellent time for a little retrospection. Throughout the year we shared eleven devlogs detailing our ideas for the game and the inner workings of some systems. Have a look at the things that we’ve done.

We started  this year with specifics about gathering and processing resources from raw  materials to necessary tools. We continued this in part two, where  we focused on the end-line of production chains, which is the creation and use of high-quality items and luxury goods, along with the buildings where those will be produced, such as Smithy, Bone Carver, Jeweler or Beekeeper.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/5f064d8a44a14f32d5963812729ebabe98ad48ff.gif[/img]

What piqued your interest the most? Well, obviously, swords. In our ninth article we covered the nitty-gritty of Viking ironworking. Did you know they extracted iron from bogs? It was a deep dive into historical methods to faithfully replicate them in Viking City Builder. The next logical step was showing the whole arsenal of deadly weapons from our game, both ranged and intended for melee. Including, but not limited to: seax, spear, skeggox and mighty Dane axe. Give that one good read and perhaps tell us what weapons you personally would like to see?

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/a86fabdcfbd619cc8eb40fb9bb30ae827036ba27.gif[/img]

However, all that work and fighting gets pretty tiresome, yet Vikings still took their leisure time seriously. Besides feasting and drinking, their activities were often a combination of fun, competition and training. Things  like arm wrestling, sparring, swimming (while trying to drown each other) or board games. They also spend time caring about hygiene, taking frequent baths and combing hair.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/454cff4811da4a87fb0598d585948a2f8fb7df9f.gif[/img]

Our team also wanted to give you a sneak peek into the creative process and each department chimed in. Programmers wrote about Building System Roles, while artists presented processes of creating animations, preparing sounds and converting 2D to 3D while making the UI of the main menu.

If you haven't seen this year's devlogs yet, we encourage you to catch up!

notes.title: Raw materials part II - Devlog #17
notes.notes:
[previewyoutube=J4QEvaWlao4;full][/previewyoutube]
Greetings fellow Vikings!

This time we’re going to look again at the [b]resources of the Viking era[/b]. Last time we covered the basics of gathering, processing, and creating the final goods from the natural riches of the land and sea. Now, we'll focus on the end-line of production chains, which is the [b]creation and use of high-quality items and luxury goods[/b].

What exactly are luxury goods? Well, those are items whose possession increases the villagers' happiness or health parameters, while lowering the village's safety, since they raise the prosperity in the settlement, making it more likely to be attacked. They aren’t necessary for survival, but having them will surely increase your status and will make your settlers more satisfied.

As an example, we can use simple combs made from bones, to increase the villager's health. This may be more useful once bone tools are replaced by iron tools made in the Smithy, so the player could swap the production in the Bone Carver from tools to combs.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/d776e0daa87311a1310843d47c9753066d0fc572.gif[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/75ee22cfde5bc7253cefb31a832d04125d0ced60.gif[/img]

Jewelry to raise his or her happiness level and providing your settlers with warm shoes, leather belts, and sacks will surely make them more satisfied as long as those items last.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/1c75a631e3ffb17da42c1eaff2d1158b4fd20d24.gif[/img]
	
Luxury goods are categorized just as standard products. From simple personal items like combs, shoes, and belts, up to pottery and expensive jewelry which requires rare materials such as amber and a drop of silver currency to be made.

Just like other crafted and used items, luxury goods will get worn down during usage and eventually will break. All the granted bonuses (and hazards) towards village parameters are gone, once the luxury stuff is broken.

Besides parameters-related luxury objects, there are also advanced products that include high-quality food, clothes, and military gear. Those high-end crafts are effective in their functionality, providing more calories, extended durability, and combat statistics than their simpler counterparts.

As an example of high-end goods, we can take high-quality clothes, which give our settlers bigger bonuses and last longer, but require more work to be done.

When looking at advanced military gear, we are getting increasing combat properties for additional costs in basic resources or in adding a fancy type of steel to the craft. 

Lastly, for some more interesting food recipes, we will look at the example of a popular mead. This well-known beverage will require water, tinder, and honey that is produced by the Beekeeper. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/244bbc19fdf08dfcd031f872cb781ed883a315ef.gif[/img]

The value of those goods makes them also a great trading asset. When converted into silver or other on more needed resources on the diplomacy and trading route.

Thanks for your attention! We hope you also liked this kind of material. Let us know what you think and don't forget to join our [b]Discord[/b]!

notes.title: Implementation of sounds - Devlog #16
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/c872f80bdaf34691968a391de3a89abbad4f6c60.png[/img]

Hello fellow Vikings!

As every month, we got a devlog for you! The newest material was prepared by Maciej, our sound designer, who will tell you about sound recording for the city builder game! Have a nice read!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/d014ef79fec858556e6ea4dc304ab3658650b9dc.png[/img]

[previewyoutube=TbhARlydFV4;full][/previewyoutube]
I started the process of working on the[b] sounds for Viking City Builder[/b] by taking a very close look at all the Viking activities that will be presented in the game. After preparing a list of sounds, I started looking for items that would best simulate the sounds of tools, manufacturing, or mining processes. The basic assumption describing how our game should sound was the statement "it has to be natural". Therefore, all the sounds you'll hear in the game are recordings of real objects.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/04441a6dd041bc9e012506cd6a4c3cd661be605d.png[/img]

Some of them sound one-to-one. This means, for example, that when recording the sounds of chopping wood, I chopped firewood. Using two types of axes. I scored some solid cardio in the process ;)

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/992fe308d943ee590f9527610d67a5084fb67ef9.jpg[/img]

Some of the samples, however, were recorded based on sounds that only mimic what you will hear in the game. How does record digging in the mud avoid an outdoor recording session and thus a mass of unwanted sounds? Birds, combines, cars, or neighbors who just decided to mow the lawn can be a really big problem! The best solution was to "put" the mud in a wheelbarrow and then carry it and its contents to the garage. After that, all that was left was to wallow in the mud with my hands or dig with a shovel. Worked like a charm!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/5cef71c8e95aa97843b38bfca294f3d5c1eda5e0.png[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/24619cb57c1cec80cec8038224f9b51b6af9f033.png[/img]

What sounds similar to forging a helmet? A metal scoop hit with a hammer fits perfectly! Tanning leather? Old leather welding coats worked quite well! Extracting honey from a beehive? The sound of ripping oranges sounds good! I could give many more such examples, but let's move on to the next production process - a sound implementation.

During recording sessions, I always remembered to keep a lot of variety in the recorded sounds. These sounds, once they were processed and prepared for implementation, I was guaranteed that the audio you would hear in the game would be diverse. The greater the variety of samples, the more natural the perception of sound. Let's remember - "it has to be natural".

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/23b45d936197ca7211f3f686cb5e716cfc494feb.png[/img]

When preparing sounds for character animation, I created a randomly played list of sounds each time, thus avoiding the artificial repetition of the same samples. That's why the animation of one hammer strike on an anvil has about six modulated variations. When creating the sounds of work and life in buildings, I decided to use the same method. This way when you listen to the work of, for example, a Smelter you’ll never hear an identical loop of sounds.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/d014ef79fec858556e6ea4dc304ab3658650b9dc.png[/img]

Thanks for reading! We hope you liked the material about recording the sounds of the work and life of our Vikings! Remember to [b]write us your feedback and visit our Discord![/b]

notes.title: Variety of buildings and decorations - Devlog #15
notes.notes:
Dear Vikings!

It's time for another devlog! We’ve got also the information about our playtests. As you're well aware, some time ago we announced signups for playtesting on Steam. As our Team started growing our ambitions got even bigger. For the last 3 months, we held hands-off sessions with game industry veterans. We were present at Nordic Game and Gamescom. We’re honoured that people were so excited about experiencing the game. Nevertheless, we’ve gathered a lot of invaluable feedback on the game and we want to implement it! It takes time, but it’s worth it.

We decided to postpone playtests. We can't yet reveal when this will happen, as we want to be sure of the date.

Thanks for your patience!

And now let's move on to the main topic of our devlog.

[previewyoutube=oD2sXEYmZic;full][/previewyoutube]
We plan to put over 50 distinct buildings in VCB. Every one of them performs a specific role and it's necessary to achieve a functioning city, however, we want to make our settlement look different every playthrough and give players a way to express themself. Today we'll talk about measures we took to achieve that.

First of all, we're creating different models of buildings. Even with an alternate look, they'll function in the same manner. As you know, we decided against modular models and our facilities are handcrafted. Ideally, we'd like to make variations for every single one, but due to sheer volume, we're starting with those most common, which will be present in multiples like houses, warehouses, etc. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/cd6d77186742c896980bc0746678b9db58da0a06.gif[/img]

Even when picking the same model, finished construction will be different from each other. We made a system that changes finer details. For example: in the yard of the first house you built, there will be a chair, buckets and a cart, but in the second one you'll find barrels and sacks of grain. The same goes for walls - ornaments will vary from building to building. As for now, we implemented Shield Generator with different patterns and dyes. Here we'd like to ask you a question - [b]should it stay that way or would you prefer to have the whole village decorated with your colors? [/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/1fc8fb4253f477ac236b0be1aecf73f2f9d669f9.gif[/img]

Last of all (for now) are self-contained decorations. Those need to be placed by the player and (for now) we want them to be purely cosmetic. Vikings may use them in their spare time and as placeable objects, there are collisions (using gates and fences one can force settlers to change their established paths). There are different styles and stages, some are small, while others are sizable. Every one of you should find something which will satisfy your taste. notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/fcde30a6b0f2f5aea928189f54e41313fcdc5d01.png[/img]

Hello Vikings!

The UI in the Viking City Builder game is starting to take shape! We’re slowly polishing the selection of element styles, typography, or colors and today we’d like to present one of its parts, which is the Main Menu. 

As most of you probably know, the Main Menu is the UI element that you’ll see on your screen, even before you start playing the game.

When creating the various UI elements, we’re accompanied by the idea of functionality, with an effective, thematic design at the same time. 

OK, let us introduce you to the technical side. When creating a 3D game, some elements like User Interface are in 2D, but the Main Menu is a 2D Art in a 3D space.

Initially, in the process of creating the Main Menu, concept art is created, which is divided into layers such as the sky, clouds, earth, or characters.

The character’s layer must be additionally divided into small parts and scattered over the texture.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/0a952253fa7cef493355418be5cf0da04b1603b1.png[/img]

On separated parts of the texture, the mesh is cut and the UV of the island is placed and then the mesh is folded so that it looks like the previously created key.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/c7e821f59bb59311b5415c3988906771cc04e6a4.png[/img]

Summarizing the first stage of technical preparation, in the beginning, you should break Art to re-glue it.

In the next stage, a rig for characters and movable elements is created, to which the mesh is skinned (assigned).

Then the animation is created and the source file is exported and then imported into the engine.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/4afeda924a36b0b04dfb1625a8dcb92de95f2fdf.png[/img]

In the engine, a scene without lighting is prepared, with an orthographic camera and a previously prepared widget with UI added.

The mesh previously imported to the engine is added to the scene and the appropriate materials are attached to it.

The materials are unlit and all rather standard except the cloud material which has a sliding tile on one of the axis to keep the clouds moving in the loop.

[previewyoutube=7gDHfQrA0ZQ;full][/previewyoutube]
Keep in mind that the Main Menu is currently a work in progress and we’re exploring its possibilities and its best looks. Today you’ll only see an iteration here and many things may still change, so we look forward to your feedback on our Discord and social media!

notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/8a0e7e83dd4e902c3df6c264f41c50cacc550f54.png[/img]

Hello Brothers and Sisters!

Today we’d like to present you material slightly different than those we've published so far. Recently, one of our programmers - Dominik - volunteered to prepare a programming devlog. We thought 'why not' and let him take the initiative ;)

So... We encourage you to check the material prepared by Dominik. You’ll find it below.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/d014ef79fec858556e6ea4dc304ab3658650b9dc.png[/img]

Earlier devlogs contained a lot of information about buildings and their functionalities. In our game, Viking City Builder, there are already a lot of them, but there will be even more of them ;) Each of these buildings is unique, you can distinguish several groups of buildings that serve different roles. Thanks to the fact, it’s easier to control it all and - if it goes well - there will be fewer bugs in the game ;) I’ll show you how it works on the example of Tailor.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/c42077fe0d60c59354bf511c7a2d4603d0679bab.png[/img]

I’ll start by showing you parameters such as Name, Icon and the 3D model that will represent this building. For the aforementioned Tailor, we can provide a 3D model of Longhouse - why not? ;)

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/7a70fbfa806c8296a8bb7dac71dc6fda89210e01.png[/img]

Now let's move on to more important issues - the functionality of this building. Roles are responsible for this, which can be freely assigned and changed. At this point you can set such details as the maximum number of workers and what profession is responsible for the work in this building.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/cda1fb3dec15d9e2d47fab7e1fc84487f0e5ab77.png[/img]

In the Tailor building, resources are exchanged for others. In Viking City Builder, the Converter role is responsible for this.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/3a4f29d74480cc341200e4c778f127014026809e.png[/img]

Production processes define what specific resources are converted into what, in what quantities and how much labor this requires. For example: 3 x Yarn + 40 labor units = 1 clothing.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/0d51508de2415ed654e42c5135128125833ca376.png[/img]

The Converter role will also automatically create a backroom role - in this case, we don’t need to set it up specifically. This will provide the building with a warehouse in which to store resources.

Now the code will automatically convert the building definition (not only the list of building instructions but also the building operation logic) at the time of construction to the actual building logic, so there’s no need to manually update it later.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/d014ef79fec858556e6ea4dc304ab3658650b9dc.png[/img]

Do you remember which building is mentioned in Dominik's text? If not, this is what Tailor will look like in our game.

notes.title: Vikings free time - Devlog #12
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/ef775e7f97f981e0244ad9702a9c461e51cb18be.png[/img]

Hello Vikings! 

Viking society wasn't only about work and raids. Their community was also built upon games and competitive sports that tested the most important attributes for the Vikings, like strength, speed and durability. Those competitions were meant to be challenging, as they were a way to train skills and hone abilities. 

Usually, Vikings were competing between each other and their games often defined winner and loser. Besides that, it served as entertainment for the spectators. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/454cff4811da4a87fb0598d585948a2f8fb7df9f.gif[/img]

While most of you may instantly think of some simple, strength or speed-based competitions like armwrestling, sparring or running, Vikings also had less physical and more brain-based games, including hnefatafl, which was a popular board-game.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/5faa0b96566712ce55551e95d6158435d50961e3.gif[/img]

If that, for some reason, didn’t sound very “attractive”, don’t worry! We are talking about Vikings after all and how could we talk about their sports without a dose of brutality? One of the more extreme “sports” was the drowning competition, which basically meant that the participants would take turns in holding their opponent under the water as long as possible.

Of course, Vikings not only spend their free time competing against each other. They also had a bunch of relaxing and safe activities.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/42cfd255354a9160f0967f8ba31c7f038f60f0c0.gif[/img]

Being a decently hygienic society, Vikings took a bath at least once per week (yes, at their times it was pretty often). One of their favorite methods of relaxing baths were hot springs. You can find your settlers chilling there, while also increasing their health.

notes.title: Vikings and their clothes - Devlog #11
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/52623479460f740dc7f5733673248795b793c412.png[/img]

Hello Vikings! 

Here’s the latest devlog! This time we'll tell you a bit about [b]Viking clothing[/b] and how they [b]obtained materials[/b] for them. Curious? We invite you to read it!

Contrary to popular belief, Vikings were not clad in leather and furs from head to toe. That said, it still was used to produce some parts of their wardrobe - mostly outer garments like shoes, belts, poaches, caps and cloaks. However, they mostly used linen and wool to make their shirts, trousers and dresses.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/bca277ff90be2a439379e4ec24d94f9e2079361c.gif[/img]

Those two materials were obtained by processing flax and fleece respectively. In our game, the players can make a choice which of the two they will use to spin yarn. This interchangeable production allows them to take into account external conditions like infertile soil to optimize the whole production process, which takes place in the [b]Spinning Mill[/b]. After harvest, flax had to be retted then threshed into fiber. Fleece, after sheep shearing, was boiled and cleaned. Both of those smelled horribly, so it would be wise to distance them from any living space. After that, fibers had to be combed before spinning using a spindle with attached whorl - disc with a hole in it. All of this hard work just to produce yarn.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/64e4017a639e315bb7b6d413437b230a22fe5a8c.gif[/img]

That's where [b]Tailor[/b] comes in. Here fabric was woven on a vertical loom going from top towards the ground. Warp threads were weighted down by stones and could be rearranged using heddle rods to create a variety of patterns. New weft was pushed towards the fabric above with a beater that was usually made of wood. While the job was both demanding and tedious this method allowed them to weave cloth with required width (typical size of the loom from the period was about 200x165 cm) to reduce waste of material through cutting. Pieces were then sewn together using needles made from bone or wood to produce clothes and sails. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/76724983a0f2830db6b640e06a847793a2e372ce.gif[/img]

Finished product could be further improved. Either  by embroidery or by dyes, which could be applied at almost any part of production. While limited in number, many of them were bright, which again is in contrast with the popular image of Vikings. Such improvements obviously involved additional costs and time. As such it was easy to differentiate the status of a person by judging their clothes, even if the method used to produce them was the same both for Karl and a Thrall. The latter probably had garments made of coarser and undyed fabric. Rich Jarls would distinguish them further with clothes embroidered with precious metals like silver or gold or even silk trims(often a grave good for high status deceased).

notes.title: Tools of War - Devlog #10
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/d12ba8ed6a8a59ccb37e9e91a0276512e85e1ed9.png[/img]

So we made a sword, but how can we use it?

Less obvious answer is trading it ;) Limited evidence on the monetary value of swords shows they were valuable or even priceless commodities. That's why they were often named (for example Leggbitr “Leg-Cleaver”) and perceived.to possess supernatural abilities. Most famous among them are ULFBERHT swords - inscripted blades, mostly excavated in Norway and around Baltic area. Those are high quality weapons, shrouded in mystery. Different variations and inscriptions suggest some were trying to counterfeit them.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/b95e9b42f4f4b4baaadd8b67b14d659a6738c9c3.jpg[/img]
[i]VLFBERHT inscription on a blade, Credit: Martin Kraft [url=https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0]CC BY-SA 3.0[/url][/i]

Obviously a sword, with its costs and significance, isn't the only weapon available, so we intend to provide you with many other tools of war. Seax, spear, skeggox or mighty dane axe - each with different characteristics allowing players to adapt their forces to match specific enemies. Our arsenal also includes ranged weapons like bows, throwing axes and spears. Although we realize that the latter could be disputed by some, there are enough mentions in sagas that we decided to include those to enrich gameplay.

[previewyoutube=D846QRoTc6w;full][/previewyoutube][i]Showcase of ingame models[/i]

But why would we need all those weapons? Well, those were dark and perilous times. Vikings, due to their superior ships and naval traditions, were the supreme raiders,  but they could also fall prey if unprepared. Arming your warriors and posting guards will be sufficient in the early stages, but with increased prosperity one needs to secure it from jealous neighbors. To this end we aim to provide many options to safeguard your hoard and subjects. Among them: walls, lookouts, palisades (including underwater!), ditches, signal fires, alarm horns - anything one needs to repel potential threats.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/b4be0a16ac52c0d6cfc286911a0a644f06fc7572.gif[/img]
[i]Not everything can be safe inside the settlement[/i]

notes.title: From swamp to sword! - Devlog #9
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/d567b69a827487b30c46506fa3bd96276f3b31dc.png[/img]

Recently, we talked about basic raw materials and where they are extracted. Probably many of you wondered what can be done with them next. Therefore, today you’ll learn how to make a [i]sword[/i]. As you could read in the previous devlogs (”Things that surprised me” - #4 & ”Raw materials part I" - #8), the first step is to get the [i]bog iron[/i]. Thrall cuts out peat cubes from bog and then burns them to obtain pea-sized ore particles.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/ed0476120cd61faf7b9c7ae7c66ddbe0c16e66fe.gif[/img]
[i]PeatMine[/i]

These go to Smelter, where they are melted into “bars” in  clay kilns. The melting point of iron is ~1500 C, so charcoal was needed to reach the right temperature. The quantity of product obtained was significantly influenced by the capabilities of the smelter, from the correct design of the furnace to the correct ratio of fuel, ore and air supply.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/063b6f40899797aa3f4ee81fc3b3b0ac6d7009ff.gif[/img]
[i]Smelter[/i]

“Where did the charcoal come from all of a sudden”, you might ask? And then comes Charcoal Kiln. Here the lengthy process of producing charcoal takes place. Pieces of wood are carefully stacked into a pile, which is then covered with a ~30 cm layer of clay. Stack is ignited through the remaining holes, which  are  filled later. Charcoal Kiln requires constant monitoring. The combustion temperature is controlled by covering cracked spots or, conversely, by punching holes in order to supply air. Depending on the size of the pile and type of wood, burning may take several days.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/7796c1b6f27306f85360fda499e783cfd456fd09.gif[/img]
[i]Charcoal Kiln[/i]

Only now, with these two necessary resources, Smithy can begin production. The specific costs of an item vary, depending on the chosen product, but the basis for each of them is already known to us: iron and charcoal. In this case, we expect a typical Nordic sword. Maybe it would be better to choose tools to ensure a consistent quality of work, but with a sword we've access to every resource in the world, right? ;)

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/55609c4416c5d43c3c59644e289f2d7d8949d9a8.gif[/img]
[i]Smithy[/i]

And so the first iron object was created in your settlement. Ultimately, it needed five different resources, three of which we can extract and two of which we've to produce using the raw materials that we've previously taken from nature.

notes.title: Raw materials part I - Devlog #8
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/18ff1c27e0d384ef9fbe0ad9526a861389e88a29.png[/img]

Greetings fellow Vikings! 

This part of the devlog will be devoted to the mechanics describing collection and processing of collected resources. From basic and vital resources to fancy and rarest materials like Damascus steel, our development team strives to reflect the real conditions and methods that the Vikings used to obtain and process their materials.

The design of each of the production chains is preceded by an in-depth historical research. Thanks to many hours spent with various historical sources, we can faithfully reproduce the entire process - of course, as much as the game mechanics allow us to ;)

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/d014ef79fec858556e6ea4dc304ab3658650b9dc.png[/img]

From obtaining the resource to creation of the final product, the entire procedure has been carefully designed to reflect the spirit of a functioning Viking settlement as closely as possible.

All sources of the materials obtained during the game are based on the actual deposits that existed at that time. For example, bog iron, essential for the production of iron, is mined in swamps as it was in reality. Of course, all deposits have a limited amount of resources they contain, and their availability and abundance of minerals depends on the map on which the game is played. For example, a settlement built on the "Birka" map will offer easier access to water and more building space than the mountainous "Kaupang" area, which in turn is richer in stone deposits. Sometimes players aiming to gather specific resources will need to work in various ways like trading or plundering.

The player will be able to adapt his playstyle to the conditions on the map. The selection of appropriate production chains, control over the resource flow and use of available raw materials will allow for the effective utilization of the riches ​​of each area.

The resources available in the game can be divided into several categories in terms of their purpose and rarity. The first category will be food, which includes both basic products obtained in the first stages of the game, such as mushrooms or blackberries, to items that require production, such as bread or mead. This category also includes all commodities required to produce food, such as wheat.

[previewyoutube=DCGnW8yrXcg;full][/previewyoutube]

Building materials are another category of raw resources. Starting with the basic ones, such as clay, wood or stone, and ending with those requiring production, such as iron, which is also an industrial resource - used in the production of various goods.

Industrial items and resources, such as the aforementioned iron, will serve in the production chains as required elements to create a finished product.

Luxury goods and armaments, both weapons and armor, make up the bundle of end products on which the resource processing chain closes. Thus, in the simplest way, the production of goods can be represented in several steps: obtaining raw materials - processing raw materials - creating a product.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/d014ef79fec858556e6ea4dc304ab3658650b9dc.png[/img]

Introducing you to the whole range of developer tasks that make up the design of the above-mentioned production chains, the following stages of work are presented:

1. Research on historical sources - the first point of design. Here we check how the processing of a specific resource looked like in the times of the Vikings.

2. Next comes creating the basic logic simulation: 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/a6f7d4be08f0b3ab1c11ed2b2bc6eba1fd14c467.png[/img]

After that we implement the idea on the model and tweak the mechanics to fit in our game.

[url=https://discord.gg/yenDAYP5Ux][img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/2724474b3f8a17c90fc924bcb14e6935f4553e22.gif[/img][/url]

Thank you for your interest in seeing how the resource design process works! We hope that the material was interesting and brought you a little closer to the details of working on Viking City Builder.

Referring to my team. You often ask me how we're doing. Let me just say, it's great! The team I am currently working with on Viking City Builder are true professionals and passionate. Every day they prove to me that I could not have made a better choice. And although we've been working together for a short time, it wouldn't be all of this without them. [b]Guys, thanks so much for this![/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/d014ef79fec858556e6ea4dc304ab3658650b9dc.png[/img]

Ok, let's get to the main topic of this devlog ;) This time we’d like to tell you about the process of making animations and show you some of them.

The animations created during the development process, which ultimately reside in the game engine, [b]begin their process with the character model.[/b] A character that has been modeled and textured should be painted with weights assigned to specific bone.This allows us to move the limbs with the bones according to the movements that can replicate the correct movement of the character from a physiological point of view. The character's skeleton itself is simplified relative to human physiology, while retaining appropriate mechanics. We additionally use "helper" bone to move the character, which control the skeleton hierarchy. With this technology (inverse kinematics), we can control one bone that affects the others. Application example: hand bending, where using two bones we influence the other bones that interact in a hierarchy relative to each other. This technique allows for a more accurate and much faster implementation.
[previewyoutube=PagiTh4Toa4;full][/previewyoutube]
The combination of the above bone mechanics is called a "rigg," which controls each bone contained in the skeleton. Controlling a character's movement involves keying frames of video to the correct location in three-dimensional space, which is assigned to the appropriate place in the timeline. This allows us to control the trajectory of bone movement and its duration. The corresponding set of keyframes of bone movement form an animation. To best replicate the movement of the characters we use recordings of ourselves performing specific actions. This makes it as close as possible to the natural structure of human movement phases. Animations are made in external software and then the whole is assembled in the engine, combining previously made animations.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/d014ef79fec858556e6ea4dc304ab3658650b9dc.png[/img]

And moving from theory to practice: below is a finished animation on the engine showing [b]Saltmaker[/b].

[previewyoutube=0Dz7baPNWLw;full][/previewyoutube]
Salt was important and expensive resource used for preservation of food. It could be obtained through trading or by evaporating water either from the sea (while seawater on average contains 3% salt, Baltic Sea has a salinity of 0.3 to 0.9%) or saline springs using lead pans. Latter source was preferred because of higher yield which is reflected by “wich” towns of Droitwich in Worcestershire, Nantwich, Middlewich and Northwich established by Romans near salt springs in Britain. Anyway, the process was time and fuel consuming, so a clever leader should perhaps look for other sources of this treasure - like foreign lands filled with soft people ;)  

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/d014ef79fec858556e6ea4dc304ab3658650b9dc.png[/img]

I hope you made it to the end. Let us know how you liked such material. Don't forget to check out our Discord, where there's also a lot going on.

See you soon!

notes.title: Brothers and Sisters, Season's Greetings! - Devlog #6
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/157042b678c0fd10b5181cecc731bf4ad82f69e6.png[/img]

Hello Vikings!

It's December, for many of us it is a special time of the year, when we live the holidays, enjoy the winter. When I recently started to wonder what I could tell you about in the next devlog, I thought about the Vikings' lives during the winter. I’ll also show you some nice shots.

Ok, let's get down to business and start with Yule - a pagan festival celebrated by Germanic peoples began on the winter solstice and lasted 12 days. How many Nordic holidays were associated with feasting, drinking and making offerings - "wassail" is a word that I didn’t know and needed in my life.

One specific ritual was the Yule Log. A log of ash, which had to be cut or given as a gift (never bought!), was set on fire using a piece of last year's trunk and allowed to glow for the duration of the festival. The ashes obtained in this way were said to ward off evil spirits, fate and disease.

Traditionally, the sacrifice was a wild boar - Sonargöltr, in the bristles of which the so-called oaths were made. Heitstrenging such as Harald Fairhair swore to not cut his hair until he became king of united Norway. Supposedly, some of these traditions still function in Scandinavia (perhaps some of you could confirm or explain), such as Yule goat. Nowadays, it's associated with a straw Christmas tree ornament tied with a red ribbon, but it used to be associated with fertility rituals or Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjóstr - goats harnessed to Thor's chariot. Many pagan traditions have been integrated with Christian holidays under the doctrine of Interpretatio Christiana. For example, Norway's King Haakon the Good made a law to move Yule to December 25. The saga of his life in Heimskringla speaks of 3 days of celebration, so he changed not only the start date but also the duration. Who knows, maybe Santa Claus is Odin in disguise.

However, winter isn’t just a time for feasting. Above all, you had to treat it with respect and prepare for it accordingly. 1000 years ago there were no shops, norse people had to rely on themselves. In the autumn, the animals were slaughtered, partly to reduce the amount of fodder needed, but also so that the resulting meat could be used as supplies. Many methods of preservation were used, such as drying, salting or smoking. Take a look at the [b]Smokehouse[/b] below. In Viking City Builder, it’s a building that ensures longer use of food products, mainly useful in preparation for winter.

[previewyoutube=eJdegVGEZ7w;full][/previewyoutube]
The grains were stored, the vegetables were buried, the milk was turned into butter or skyr. The building that produces dairy products from the resource you receive is called [b]Dairy[/b]. This is what it will look like in my game. 

[previewyoutube=7O3kMrTnGiY;full][/previewyoutube]
Beer was brewed, fuel was collected in advance. The building that produces alcoholic beverages from the resources provided is [b]Brewery[/b]. Here's what this object will look like in Viking City Builder.

[previewyoutube=bbafkhmmQsQ;full][/previewyoutube]
The proper management of stocks and the year-round collection of these were decisive for the life and death of the inhabitants. 

It was difficult to move in the land covered with ice and covered with snow. Today we associate ice skating, skis and sleighs with winter fun. While norse people also used the above-mentioned for sports, they were used primarily as a means of transport. Ice skates were most often made of bone and tied to shoes. The skis differed in length, one long skid - a skid and the other short - drive. They used a lunar calendar, where a month had one cycle of moon phases, and winter was one of the two seasons (the other being of course summer). Of course, you have to take into account geographical discrepancies - the Danes felt the seasons differently than their northern brothers. The higher the latitude, the more the effects of polar days and nights were felt. To this day, it’s a problem that the Swedes and Norwegians solve through exposure and trips south. Some compensation is the opportunity to experience the Northern Lights or Aurora Borealis. Surprisingly, no reference to Viking mythology can be found in reliable sources. Some claim that the lights were reflections or glow from armour of the Valkyries, but that's more along the lines of wishful thinking or so called modern interpretation.

Ok, that would be it for a devlog. Whereas…

My Dear Vikings, regardless of who and to whom you will spend the end of December, I wish you that this time will be filled with joy, health and peace. May the Gods protect you and send you many favors!

Roslagen

notes.title: Death and burial in the Viking world - Devlog #5
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/bca7699a688b59d705aa585025d3718c17a5a482.png[/img]

Hello, Vikings!

Halloween is approaching, and while the holiday itself doesn't have much to do with Vikings, it is quite strongly associated with death. This inspired me to create a devlog with a slightly darker theme, about death and burial in the Viking world.

Many concepts about what happens to people after death have been forgotten or misrepresented over the years. Surely all of you have heard of Valhalla - the hall of the slain, where the Valkyries took their fallen warriors, where they feasted and competed in anticipation of Ragnarök. Another place that some readers are aware of is Helheim ruled by Hel, where those who died of sickness, old age and cowards were said to end up. Sailors dying at sea with their treasures ended up in the Coral Caves of Rán. Some of the dead were created as Draugr - a type of undead being. But who among you has heard of Fólkvangr ("the field of the people" or "the field of warriors")? It was ruled by Freyja, and half of the warriors killed in battle were sent there, which the goddess selected together with Odin. The discovery was quite a surprise to me. I wondered if the idea of Fólkvangr came about as a result of the integration of the Aesir and Vanir pantheonsand why was it almost forgotten compared to Valhalla, which we have all heard about after all?

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/68da55842c90c9e554856d08de1ac94132b42dc5.jpg[/img]
              There are worse places to go when you die, Valhalla (1905) by Emil Doepler


So much for the widely understood hereafter. However, the body of the deceased must be taken care of first. What were their funeral traditions like, apart from the fact that most of them involved lavishly drunken feasts ;) The first thing that comes to mind is a dead Jarl resting on a boat, which was then set on fire and pushed out onto the water. While the custom of burning boats existed (I recommend Ahmad ibn Fadlan's description) it was much more common to bury the dead in boats. However, a ship is a precious thing, so boat-shaped burial mounds were often created. However, the rituals described above had to be earned. The greys were buried in ordinary graves. Depending on the region and period, bodies were either buried whole or cremated first and then the vessel with ashes was buried. There were also "deviant burials" where corpses ended up in the grave with their heads cut off or placed face down. Although the density of the latter on Gotland may indicate a unique funerary tradition, rather than an attempt to humiliate the deceased or protect them from their spirit. Another unique curiosity is the grave of G511 at Repton. The marks on the femur indicate a severe wound that most likely resulted in the left testicle and penis. Which would explain why he was buried with a boar tusk between his thighs. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/8b9c3a2dbfb83cdac2e2c54214e4495316a40154.png[/img]
Example of stone ship Blomsholm, Sweden. Credit: Paula Molander CC BY-SA 4.0


Regardless of the method used, funeral gifts were placed in the graves. The dead were buried with objects and weapons that belonged to them or that could be useful in the hereafter (in the case of cremation these were also burned). Craftsmen were given their tools, commanders board games like Tafl, women jewelry and house keys. The amount of treasures gathered in the famous Oseberg Ship is staggering: household and agricultural tools, silks, clothes, buckets, tapiseries and even a sleigh and a cart (interestingly, supposedly the only one found)! Mention should be made of the remains of many animals - horses, dogs and oxen - which were also found there. Not only animals but also slaves were sacrificed to the dead (again I refer you to Ahmad ibn Fadlan if you haven't already) to serve their masters after death. As Christianization progressed, exhumations were reportedly made to re-bury the deceased, this time in Catholic rites. Harald Bluetooth is said to have done so at Jelling with the corpse of his father Gorm.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/c84a49e6d2a900ba1e730eb7ea3a7e4d0379a5b3.png[/img]
Jelling Royal Necropolis, credit: http://viking.archeurope.com

It would seem that with so many afterlife and various rituals the dead were not given much attention later on. Nothing could be further from the truth. In honor of those who passed away, poems were composed (e. g. Sonatorrek) or runic stones were erected dedicated to their life and circumstances of death. Hundreds of years later, the sagas were written down - stories that had been passed down through oral tradition. Evidently, however, the respect they showed to their own did not translate to strangers. An example is the Neolithic burial mound of Maeshowe - famous because of the 30 runic inscriptions with which it has been "beautified".

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/a84f4e34cf6cb468d3e0048baa0ecce1a0969790.png[/img]
Some things never change ;) Credit: http://viking.archeurope.com


Okay, that would be it for today. I hope you enjoy this theme! Or maybe you have some interesting facts about death and burial in the Viking world? If so, share them in the comments!

Happy Halloween and see you soon!

notes.title: Things that surprised me - Devlog #4
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/c9727734f1087587d7c34f36f91b18175f84d84a.png[/img]

Hello, my dear Vikings.

In the beginning, I would like to thank you for such a positive reception of the previous devlog. Just to remind you that its topic was the locations that inspired me while creating the game. It was an interesting experience for me because, on one hand, I took a sentimental journey to the times when I lived in Scandinavia while writing it, and I must say that it was a great period in my life. On the other hand, I could show you a different aspect of development - research. Today I'm going to continue this thread and tell you about what surprised me while working on Viking City Builder.

Going back to the last devlog for a moment I mentioned Kaupang among the locations I want to put in Viking City Builder. What shocked me is that even though the terrain has not changed, the difference in sea level is noticeable to the naked eye. I had to raise the water level in the engine to replicate this historical location.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/54e2d02f6cdfec11d754eddefe775be7d21df962.png[/img]
[i]On the left model, the area that is currently land is marked in light green. On the right, for comparison, you can see the "historical" look in UE4. Credit: Model of the Viking town Kaupang, Vestfold © 2005 J. P. Fagerback[/i] www.aftenposten.no

It turns out that the image from pop culture is quite different from reality. As an example, there are horned helmets, which many of you have noticed while watching the trailer I've prepared :)

Contradictory to the vision of a wild, tumbled and dirty invader are archaeological findings, but also contemporary descriptions of them. In his chronicle, St. John of Wallingford, Prior of St. Fridswides bitterly recalled the Danes who, "combing their hair daily, bathing every day and changing their clothes frequently, were able to undermine the virtues of married women and even seduce the daughters of noblemen". It's very far away from the vision of a wild, dirty invader that may arise in your mind while reading contemporary descriptions. One of the stanzas from Hávamál (a series of poems containing advice on life, proper behavior, and knowledge) mentions the custom of washing hands before meals. Being neglectful was rather associated with people in a state of mourning. They had tools such as a comb, ear spoon, tweezers, pick and nail cleaners at their disposal. They bathed in rivers, but they also built bathhouses and used hot springs.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/fb2bd532fc11414a7228b9f97e60f22674857840.png[/img] [i]Bone combs are one of the most commonly found artifacts from Viking times. Credit: [/i]https://stock.adobe.com/pl/

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/ab72e0d5c99d49eefb8b3e706881e4856d244b1d.png[/img]
[i]Bath built by Snorri Sturluson at his farm at Reykholt Credit:[/i] https://stock.adobe.com/pl/

Another thing that amazed me was the extent of their expansion. Not just in terms of trade contacts, but also setting up places where they lived permanently. While I was aware that they've settled on all sorts of islands in the North Sea, as well as Iceland and Greenland, the settlements in America and far eastern Europe surprised me. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/775aec15de57f47afd28f0584752be2c7188ac6e.png[/img]
[i]Would you dare cross the Atlantic in something like that? Credit:[/i] https://stock.adobe.com/pl/

According to the Russian Primary Chronicle: “6370 (862 BC)… Discord thus ensued among them, and they began to war one against another. They said to themselves, 'Let us seek a prince who may rule over us, and judge us according to the law.' They accordingly went overseas to the Varangian Rus: these particular Varangians were known as Rus, just as some are called Swedes, and others Normans, Angles, and Goths, for they were thus named. The Chuds, the Slavs, and the Krivichians then said to the people of Rus: 'Our whole land is great and rich, but there is nor order in it. Come to rule and reign over us.' They thus selected three brothers, with their kinfolk, who took with them all the Rus, and migrated. The oldest, Rurik, located himself in Novgorod; the second, Sinaeus, in Beloozero; and the third, Truvor, in Izborsk. On account of these Varangians, the district of Novgorod became known as Russian (Rus) land. The present inhabitants of Novgorod are descended from the Varangian race, but a long time ago they were Slavs.”   
	
The Byzantine emperors recruited Vikings into their famous Varangian Guard. Many famous Norsemen served in it, including Kolskegg Hamundarsson and King Harald Hardrada.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/ddcc86592549877f6ce64490391a6f0420e0a55a.png[/img]
[i]The size of the Scandinavian diaspora is staggering. Credit: [/i]http://viking.archeurope.com

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/ae05486ef42b6439333808fc130d30c14fd5ebdd.png[/img]
[i]Location of Novgorod and Beloozero. Red and blue lines indicate trade routes Geoffrey Barraclough, ed. (in dutch) (1981) Spectrum-Times Atlas van de Wereldgeschiedenis, pp. 114–115[/i]

One of the more mundane, literally and figuratively, curiosities concerns their source of iron. It turns out that in addition to importing iron, they've obtained it from swamps. The so-called bog iron granules were extracted by cutting down peat. What is more interesting, due to the process of creation, this source was renewable. That is why many settlements were established near peat bogs.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/f6ff435e451e14d118b9d41b7d49d100d9c09609.png[/img]
[i]Natural oily layer on the surface of seeping water in a peat area that is produced by the iron-oxidizing bacteria ones the iron-rich water from the underground contacts with air. Credit:[/i] https://stock.adobe.com/pl/

Ok, that's enough for today. I hope you will learn a lot of new things about Vikings from this video and like it as much as the prior devlog.

notes.title: Areas that I’ve been inspired - Devlog #3
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/faf94e892f920a4baeba0f0903e654e902291cf0.png[/img]

Hello, fellow Vikings!

It's been a while since we've heard from each other, and I know I've neglected Steam a bit, but I’ve decided it’s time to finally get back to you. Unfortunately, working on the game consumes all my time. Recently I showed you [b]some screenshots of landscapes[/b] that will appear in my game on my social media channels. Looking at them, I thought, "Dude, you did a great job. This looks better than real life." Yes, I know, it sounds very bold of me, but considering how much effort and time I’ve put into it, I felt really satisfied with the results.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/bd94031bdea644ac5a80ed6098ff3f88e0eed895.png[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/78108aba9dfcddb46eee1690325b4a244d84753f.png[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/49ab7641ff33982dd3db01487b03179788e77c93.png[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/048d2f0595c2cd9f8f3b510b0f435bbc236d28df.png[/img]
[i]Some screenshots from my game, showing the fjords[/i]

I also thought it would be fun to give you some insight into the [b]areas that I’ve been inspired by and that are close to my heart.[/b]

[b]Scandinavia[/b] is an incredibly beautiful place. This is the region of northern Europe, that covers Sweden, Norway and Denmark. I don't know if you’re aware, I might have already mentioned this, I’m a great fan of Nordic culture. It was an amazing experience for me, to see the places where the Vikings used to live and work with my own eyes. Inherent and perhaps most distinctive element of the Scandinavian landscape are the fjords – mystical, fairy tale-like structures. In reality fjords are deep bays, strongly cut into the land with a distinct steep banks. They were formed by a retreating glacier during the last Pleistocene glaciation period.

It's a truly breathtaking sight when you see them for the first time in your life. During my first encounter with the fjords, I could see all those drakkars that the Vikings used to sail out to conquer the world with my mind’s eye. Oh yes, the [b]fjords are definitely a place where people can feel the ancient Viking Spirit.[/b] During my stay in Scandinavia I had the opportunity to see several fjords, but the most memorable was Sognefjorden - the largest fjord in Europe and the second largest in the world. It’s 203 km long and has a maximum depth of 1308 km.

Okay, let's get down to business.

Traditionally, Vikings have settled in places that met at least two of several criteria. Among the important factors there were: access to the sea (direct or via a river), the intersection of trade routes, the relief of the terrain to facilitate defence, and above all, access to food, drinking water and other resources. I had to face the daunting tasks of recreating [b]all those factors on the game maps using Unreal Engine.[/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/9cf8386efa26226fc8dfad6cfb0cc1d5c1ad20fa.png[/img]
[i]Aerial view of former Hedeby at the end of Schlei. Credit: [/i]http://viking.archeurope.com

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/6fafe2024c4a457d69302b07650d3f125c3f6e97.png[/img]
[i]Birka Hillfort was located on the top of the mound. Credit: [/i]http://viking.archeurope.com

After familiarizing myself with the tools I got carried away by my imagination and started making a test map, the screenshots of which you have already seen. Unfortunately, I lost my spirit, so I started looking for the inspiration among the places where the Vikings lived 1000 years ago. It was then that I had an epiphany. Why not use the elevation maps of the above-mentioned areas and not reproduce their topography and coordinates? 

The [b]island of Björkö[/b] came first. I chose it because the famous [b]Birka settlement[/b] was located there, and also because there had been little to no changes made by man since the Viking Age.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/7d32744c37f6306cfcb429c070d95feecca1497a.png[/img]
[i]The cross of Ansgar raised in 1834 in commemoration of Christian missionary and his short lived congregation in Birka. Credit:[/i] https://www.shutterstock.com/pl/image-photo/monument-ansgar-erected-1834-on-swedish-514784344

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/837d90a32ec3d564a4baa8d63e1379c027e6a6c4.png[/img]
[i]Which of these images is a photo and which is a screen shot from the game?[/i]

The game will allow you to modify the difficulty level which will depend on the place you have chosen for your settlement. This will be manifested through climatic differences - the fertility of the fields and the length of the winter, economic differences - the availability and quantity of various raw materials such as quarries in Hyllestad, and political differences - relations with neighbours and distance from potential raid targets. The list of starting locations will include settlements in Scandinavia, as well as the [b]islands of Baltic, Shetlands, Faroe and Orkney.[/b] Those of you better acquainted with history will surely notice the absence of a few places more distant from the cradle, but as for them I have other plans, which I will talk about in the future. Although those familiar with the topic can certainly guess what's on my mind.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/e9852428a1b190d2866b48193b3fccac98d4e31e.png[/img]
[i]Brough of Deerness, Orkney. Credit:[/i] http://viking.archeurope.com

So, in short, if you ever wanted to go to Scandinavia, I highly recommend it. In the meantime, I’ll try my best to show you, through my game, what I have experienced during my trips.

Let me know what you think about it. I hope you like it.

In the meantime, I'm going back to work so I can write to you soon with even more content!

Hope to see you soon!

notes.title: Viking Warrior Woman
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/87a5ea66d58f096dfafa4a6496ca01fdbfa830b8.png[/img]
[i]drawing by Tancredi Valeri[/i]

[b]Introduction[/b]
Researching authentic Viking Life is not an easy task. Most of our knowledge comes from one of 3 sources: archeological findings, contemporary descriptions made mostly by Catholics, and Icelandic sagas, made a few hundred years after the events. Even though Vikings had a runic alphabet, Futhark, they didn’t write books. They preferred oral traditions of sharing knowledge and stories. 

[b]Women of Viking Age[/b]
The International Women’s Day inspired me to write a post about a topic that baffles historians to this day: what was the life of Viking Women like? The Vikings had a big differentiation of roles between sexes. While men doing feminine things or women doing manly things was not forbidden, it was frowned upon and could lead to ostracism.

Women’s tasks included: taking care of the household, raising children, cooking meals, overseeing servants and slaves, sewing clothes, making dairy products, and brewing alcohol. The magic, Seiðr, was also a domain of women. 

[b]Ringkvinna[/b]
On the other hand Scandinavian women of the Viking Age still had much more freedom and influence compared to the other countries of early medieval Europe.

Unmarried woman would become an adult when she turned 20, gaining a right to choose a place to live and stand by herself in all juridical senses before the law. Women whose male relatives were dead could become Ringkvinna - head of the family, with all the privileges of this status. 

A good example was Aud (or Unn) the Deep Minded. After her husband Olaf the White and son Thorstein the Red died, she led a group of 20 free Vikings to Iceland, where she took control of the lands, becoming a matriarch of a powerful “family”. Her power and influence were a source of envy for many men.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/d026c87735e44322f470fa5056a985c3037e0721.png[/img]
[i]Source: [url=https://odtworcy.pl/sylwetki/wczesne-sredniowiecze/zamozna-kobieta-epoki-wikiingow/]Poczet Odtwórców Polskich[/url] [/i]

[b]Shieldmaidens[/b]
Two hot topics when speaking about Vikings are war and raids. Did Viking women fight? On one hand, Icelandic sagas describe women as non-fighting. On the other hand, the sagas would praise women that showed honor, courage, and strong will and honored women who’d take arms when the situation demanded it.

Archeology also doesn’t give us a decisive answer to that question either. In 1877 the remains of a warrior in Birka Bj 581 grave were believed to be a male warrior (even a leader), mostly due to the burial gifts inside.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/5f2ae04fa1ff8d889468ed3b4fb012ca0cbad8db.png[/img]
[i]drawing by Þórhallur Þráinsson[/i]

Until in 2017, with the use of modern research techniques, it was determined that they were remains of a woman. Archeologists to this day debate whether the burial gifts are proof of her being a warrior or were they merely a part of a ritual. The existence of some shieldmaiden seems to be possible, but how many? How often would it happen? How was it viewed by society?

[b]End thoughts[/b]
I leave you with those ideas to ponder and in the meantime, I’m going back to work on VCB. If you found any errors in my post, please do let me know. I’d love to make women an important part of my game as well, and I’m very curious about your feedback!

notes.title: Utility AI - Devlog #1
notes.notes:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/fcb1d7dc2299ed0273973b792df167e5d962527d.png[/img]

Hello, fellow Vikings! 

I know I haven’t posted too much new video content lately so I’d love to share with you what I have been up to. One of the things that excites me the most about the city builder games is the [b]simulation of living, breathing society. The citizens[/b] don’t just walk back and forth between the gold mine and the town hall, like in a [b]typical RTS game[/b]. They have homes and families. They have names, lives and interesting stories. After you set up a working economy you can watch them go around their business and start really caring. And since Nordic people of the [b]Viking Age[/b] are famous for their grit and strong will, it’s super important to me to breathe life into the citizens of Viking City Builder. 

I’ve started by playing my favourite city builders - Banished and Dawn of Man. I’ve immersed myself in those worlds and spent a lot of time watching my citizens. Then I’ve played a little less obvious inspirations of mine, like RimWorld and Frostpunk. I've also watched a lot of youtube videos on Viking life. What was their daily routine etc. 

After that I felt I know [b]WHAT[/b] I want to achieve. Now I just needed [b]HOW[/b]. How to turn my idea of Viking village life into code.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/476072ecaf015c2869b6f15761738432a25e72ea.png[/img]

To achieve what I wanted I needed a really robust AI system. My first implementation of the AI was rather straightforward - I’ve used [b]Behaviour Trees[/b] to make units do what I wanted. [b]Unreal Engine[/b] has a built in [b]BT[/b] system that is easy to use and that I am familiar with. It works great for pre-made behaviours, creating [b]Reactive AI[/b], like in Shooter or RTS games.  

But what I felt that is really needed is [b]Emergent Behaviours[/b], something that makes you believe this is an independent being, not a pre-programmed bot. I had to go deeper. So I’ve started researching. 

I’ve remembered mentions of technologies like Goal Oriented Action Planning and Utility Based AI. After reading a bit on the topic, I’ve decided Utility AI is the way to go. I don’t want this post to become a book so I’ll try to briefly explain what Utility AI is.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38753827/c575fa2f0f6506fea2e4449d0489561049b19c8e.png[/img]

Imagine you have a game like [b]The Sims[/b]. Your sim has few needs - let’s say hunger, sleep, hydration and entertainment. So how would you program your Sim making a decision what to do next? If you used Behaviour Trees or other Decision Tree approaches you would have to code a lot of cases: if you are super hungry and not tired - eat pizza. But if you are a bit hungry and super tired - maybe sleep first and then eat pizza. Now imagine having to pre-program all those behaviours for the game.

What [b]Utility Based AI[/b] does is allow you to create a [b]fitness function[/b] - a function that takes some considerations and produces a number for each of the decisions. E.g. for eating pizza you could create a function like: “desire to eat pizza = 5 * hunger + 2 * boredom - 10 * size of my belly” ;) You get the point.

This is exactly what I needed. Unfortunately there is no built-in Utility AI framework in Unreal, so now I spend my time between reading whitepapers on Utility AI and trying to implement it in Unreal. So you know - if you ever feel like I’m not that active on social media - it might just be that I’m trying to figure out the best fitness function for eating pizza ;)

[b]Hello, Vikings! I’ve collected the most frequently asked questions about Viking City Builder. Read through and make sure there isn't an issue here that you would like to ask about. Stay tuned![/b]

[h3][b]When will the game be released?[/b][/h3]
[i]Unfortunately, at this point in the development process, I can't say exactly, when the game will be released. I’m doing my best to make it happen as soon as possible. Stay tuned![/i]

[h3][b]How much will that game cost?[/b][/h3]
[i]I’ll be able to tell you the price of the game a moment before its release. [/i]

[h3][b]Is it true that only one person is working on Viking City Builder?[/b][/h3]
[i]Of course, it’s true. I wish I had a big team to finish this game quicker, but I’m an indie developer, so I have to do the best I can. I'm using some assets from a marketplace to speed up the development, which is a common practice in Indie Games.[/i]

[h3][b]What platforms will this game be available on?[/b][/h3]
[i]I plan to release the game on PC and you will be able to buy it on Steam. I'm also considering a console version.[/i]

[h3][b]Will the game have any demo/prologue? If so, will it be free?[/b][/h3]
[i]I can assure you that such a demo or prologue will be released and it will be for free.[/i]

[h3][b]Will there be beta testing? If so, how will it be possible to apply to them?[/b][/h3]
[i]At this point, I'm not looking for anyone to test, but as soon as the opportunity arises I'll be sure to let you know via my social media.[/i]

[h3][b]What engine was used in the game?[/b][/h3]
[i]Unreal Engine was used in the game.[/i]

[h3][b]Will there be a multiplayer mode in the game?[/b][/h3]
[i]At this point, I have no plans to introduce a multiplayer mode in Viking City Builder.[/i]

[h3][b]Does the game have its Discord server?[/b][/h3]
[i]Not yet, but don't worry, the game will definitely have Discord.[/i]

[i]Next to the release date, this is probably one of the most frequently asked questions. So. . . To answer: why helmets with horns? As a big fan of Norse mythology and Viking culture, I have to admit that your comments are correct that the image of a Viking wearing a helmet with horns is not historically accurate. I’ve used it so the people instantly recognize the vikings on the screenshots and videos, and the horned helmets are very recognizable. But in the final version of the game I’d love to be true to historical sources and find other ways to convey the Viking spirit.[/i]

[i]I bought the music for the trailer from a paid soundtrack site. Link: [b][url=https://audiojungle.net/item/viking-raid/7402280]HERE[/url][/b].[/i]

[i]Adding my game to your list is the biggest support for me because it increases its visibility on Steam. If you haven't already done so, I'd love it if you added it. This will help me a lot on my way to releasing the game.[/i]
